It’s not going to be an easy ride, but I’m ready to learn all the tricks involved. Like the current leaders in Nepal, who rode to power through rhetoric and gimmicks, I’m planning to use those same tactics to my advantage.

Once in power, I will make up for all the suffering I had to endure in my past life. I do not know what I’ll do to those who harmed me.

articles.title: एमाले कसैको सहारामा उभिने ‘लहरो’ होइन, आफैंमा बलियो ‘वृक्ष’ हो: ओली
articles.summary:
नेकपा (एमाले) का अध्यक्ष केपी शर्मा ओलीले आफ्नो पार्टी अरू कसैको सहारामा मात्र उभिने ‘लहरो’ नभएको बताएका छन्।

एमाले आफ्नै बलमा हुर्किएको र अनेकौं राजनीतिक उतारचढाव सामना गरेर स्थापित भएको एक स्वतन्त्र ‘वृक्ष’ भएको उनको दाबी छ।

संसदीय कामकारबाहीलाई प्रभावकारी बनाउने सन्दर्भमा आइतबार आयोजित छलफल कार्यक्रमलाई सम्बोधन गर्दै अध्यक्ष ओलीले यस्तो धारणा राखेका हुन्।

पार्टीको सङ्घर्षशील इतिहासबारे बोल्दै अध्यक्ष ओलीले भने, ‘एमाले कुनै अरूको सहारामा मात्र उभिने लहरो होइन, आफ्नै बलमा उम्रेको, हुर्केको र अनेकौं आँधी हुरी, तुफान तथा बाढीको सामना गरेर दह्रो बनेको एक स्वतन्त्र वृक्ष हो।’

छलफलका क्रममा उनले संसद्मा पार्टीको भूमिकालाई थप जनमुखी र प्रभावकारी बनाउनुपर्नेमा समेत जोड दिएका थिए।

articles.title: विश्वकप फाइनलमा अर्जेन्टिनालाई नेतान्याहूको साथ
articles.summary:
इजरायलका प्रधानमन्त्री बेन्जामिन नेतान्याहूले अर्जेन्टिना र स्पेनबिच हुने विश्वकप फाइनलमा अर्जेन्टिनालाई समर्थन गर्ने बताएका छन्। यो समर्थन प्रकट गर्न उनले इजरायलका लागि अर्जेन्टिनाका राजदूत रब्बी शिमोन एक्सेल वाहनिशसँग भेट गरेका छन्।

भेटका क्रममा रब्बी वाहनिशले अर्जेन्टिनाका राष्ट्रपति जेभियर माइलीको सन्देश सुनाएका थिए। सो सन्देशमा माइलीले नेतान्याहूको समर्थनको प्रशंसा गरेका छन्। त्यसको जवाफमा नेतान्याहूले भने, ‘जेभियर, तिमी साथी हौ। एक सच्चा साथी। तिमी एक महान साथी हौ, हामी तिमीलाई समर्थन गर्छौं, हामी अर्जेन्टिनालाई धेरै तरिकाले समर्थन गर्छौं। शुभकामना!’

मेस्सी होइन, माइलीका कारण विश्वकपमा अर्जेन्टिनालाई समर्थन गर्छु : इजरायली प्रधानमन्त्री

उनले अधिकांश इजरायली नागरिक अर्जेन्टिनाकै पक्षमा रहेको दाबी गरेका छन्। स्पेन र अर्जेन्टिनाबिचको यो खेललाई अहिले केही मानिसले निकै चासोका साथ हेरेका छन्। यो खेललाई प्रतीकात्मक प्रतिस्पर्धाका रूपमा लिइएको छ।

सामाजिक सञ्जालमा समेत यस विषयलाई लिएर विभिन्न खालका टिप्पणी भइरहेका छन्। खेलमा अर्जेन्टिना लगातार उपाधि जित्ने दाउमा छ भने स्पेन युवा स्टार लामिन यामालको नेतृत्वमा मैदानमा उत्रिने तयारीमा छ।

articles.title: डेस्कटप ब्राउजरमा चल्न थाल्यो फेसबुक
articles.summary:
प्राविधिक अवरोधका कारण करिब डेढ घण्टा बन्द भएका सामाजिक सञ्जाल फेसबुक र इन्स्टाग्राम आइतबार दिउँसो ३: २० बजेपछि पुनः सुचारु भएका छन्।

विशेषगरी डेस्कटप ब्राउजरमा देखिएको यो समस्याका कारण विश्वभरका लाखौँ प्रयोगकर्ता प्रभावित भएका थिए।

नेपालमा आइतबार दिउँसो साढे १ बजेदेखि फेसबुक र इन्स्टाग्राम चल्न छाडेको थियो। धेरैजसो प्रयोगकर्ताले मोबाइल एपमा सेवा चलिरहे पनि डेस्कटप ब्राउजरबाट लगइन गर्दा नखुलेको गुनासो गरेका थिए।

दिउँसो ३ बजेपछि भने दुवै सञ्जाल पूर्ववत् अवस्थामा फर्किएका हुन्। अनलाइन सेवाहरूको अवस्था निगरानी गर्ने पोर्टल ‘डाउनडिटेक्टर’ का अनुसार ६३ प्रतिशत समस्या वेबसाइटमा देखिएको थियो भने २० प्रतिशत मोबाइल उपकरण र १० प्रतिशत एपमा देखिएको थियो।

articles.title: विश्वकपमा उपाधि चुम्न स्पेनको रणनीति कस्तो ?
articles.summary:
स्पेनका मुख्य प्रशिक्षक लुइस डे ला फुएन्टेले फिफा विश्वकप २०२६को फाइनलमा अर्जेन्टिनाका कप्तान लियोनल मेस्सीलाई रोक्न कुनै एक खेलाडीलाई विशेष जिम्मेवारी नदिने बताएका छन् ।

आइतबार न्युयोर्कस्थित मेटलाइफ स्टेडियममा हुने अर्जेन्टिनाविरुद्धको उपाधि भिडन्तअघि आयोजित पत्रकार सम्मेलनमा डे ला फुएन्टेले मेस्सीविरुद्ध ‘म्यान मार्किङ’ रणनीति विगतमा असफल भएको अनुभव सुनाउँदै यस्तो बताएका हुन् ।

स्पेनका प्रशिक्षकले आफूले पहिलो पटक युवा अवस्थामा खेलिरहेका मेस्सीलाई देखेको स्मरण गरे । उनले वर्षौंअघिको कोपा डेल रे प्रतियोगितामा सेभिया र बार्सिलोनाबीचको खेलमा मेस्सीलाई रोक्न आफ्नो टोलीले विशेष योजना बनाएको स्मरण गरे ।

‘मैले युवा फुटबल खेल्दा नै लियोनल मेस्सीलाई भेटेको थिएँ । त्यो सेभिया र बार्सिलोनाबीचको कोपा डेल रे खेल थियो । हामीले मेस्सीबारे धेरै सुनेका थियौँ,’ डे ला फुएन्टेले भने । उनले थपे, ‘हामीले सुरुवातमा उनलाई म्यान मार्क गर्ने निर्णय गर्‍यौँ । खेलको ७०औँ मिनेटसम्म खेल गोलरहित बराबरीमा थियो । उनलाई रोकिरहेका खेलाडीले कार्ड पाएपछि मैले उनलाई परिवर्तन गरेँ । त्यसपछि अर्को १५ मिनेटमै मेस्सीले चार गोल गरे ।’

पुरानो अनुभव सम्झँदै डे ला फुएन्टेले विश्वकप फाइनलमा पनि मेस्सीमाथि विशेष ध्यान दिइने भए पनि एक जना खेलाडीमार्फत मात्र रोक्ने योजना नरहेको स्पष्ट पारे । ‘के हामी उनलाई म्यान मार्किङ गर्नेछौँ ? होइन । तर के हामी उनीमाथि धेरै ध्यान दिनेछौँ ? हो । तर उनीहरूले पनि हाम्रा खेलाडीहरूमाथि त्यत्तिकै ध्यान दिनेछन,’उनले भने ।

स्पेनका प्रशिक्षकले अर्जेन्टिना र प्रशिक्षक लियोनल स्कालोनीको प्रशंसा गर्दै उनीप्रति आफ्नो सम्मान रहेको बताए । ‘प्रशंसा, प्रशंसा र अझ धेरै प्रशंसा,’ उनले अर्जेन्टिनाबारे भने । उनले स्कालोनीलाई आफ्नो राम्रो साथीसमेत भएको बताए ।

डे ला फुएन्टेले स्पेनका युवा स्टार लामिन यामाललाई मेस्सीसँग तुलना नगर्न आग्रह गर्दै यामाललाई आफ्नै शैलीमा विकास हुन दिनुपर्ने बताए । ‘लामिन यामाल, यामाल नै हुनुपर्छ । मेस्सी अविश्वसनीय प्रतिभा हुन् र सबै युवा खेलाडीका लागि उदाहरण हुन् । तर लामिनले आफ्नै पहिचान बनाउनुपर्छ,’ उनले भने ।

स्पेन विश्वकप २०२६ मा उत्कृष्ट लयमा रहेको छ । टोलीले अहिलेसम्म प्रतियोगितामा एक गोल मात्र खाएको छ भने एउटै विश्वकप संस्करणमा ६ क्लिन सिट राख्ने पुरुष विश्वकप इतिहासकै पहिलो टोली बनेको छ । स्पेनले लगातार ६ खेल जित्दै अस्ट्रिया, पोर्चुगल, बेल्जियम र फ्रान्सलाई पराजित गर्दै सन् २०१० पछि पहिलो पटक विश्वकप फाइनलमा स्थान बनाएको हो ।

स्पेनको टोली लगातार ३७ खेलमा अपराजित छ र आइतबार अर्जेन्टिनालाई हराउन सके युरोपेली पुरुष राष्ट्रिय टोलीको सबैभन्दा लामो अपराजित यात्राको नयाँ कीर्तिमान बनाउनेछ ।

यता साविक विश्वकप विजेता अर्जेन्टिना लगातार दोस्रो उपाधिको खोजीमा छ । सेमिफाइनलमा इंग्ल्यान्डलाई २–१ ले हराउँदै फाइनल पुगेको अर्जेन्टिनाले पछिल्ला १४ खेल लगातार जितेको छ । टोलीले खेलको अन्तिम समयमा उत्कृष्ट प्रदर्शन गर्दै ८५औँ मिनेटपछि आठ गोल गरेर प्रतियोगिताकै नयाँ कीर्तिमान बनाएको छ ।

अर्जेन्टिना र स्पेनबीचको पछिल्लो हेड–टु–हेड इतिहास बराबरी छ । दुवै टोलीले ६–६ जित निकालेका छन् भने दुई खेल बराबरीमा सकिएका छन् । त्यसैले युरोपियन च्याम्पियन स्पेन र कोपा अमेरिका विजेता अर्जेन्टिनाबीचको विश्वकप फाइनल निकै रोमाञ्चक हुने अपेक्षा गरिएको छ । एजेन्सीको सहयोगमा

articles.title: एमाले कसैको सहारामा उभिने ‘लहरो’ होइन, आफैंमा बलियो ‘वृक्ष’ हो: ओली
articles.summary:
नेकपा (एमाले) का अध्यक्ष केपी शर्मा ओलीले आफ्नो पार्टी अरू कसैको सहारामा मात्र उभिने ‘लहरो’ नभएको बताएका छन्।

एमाले आफ्नै बलमा हुर्किएको र अनेकौं राजनीतिक उतारचढाव सामना गरेर स्थापित भएको एक स्वतन्त्र ‘वृक्ष’ भएको उनको दाबी छ।

संसदीय कामकारबाहीलाई प्रभावकारी बनाउने सन्दर्भमा आइतबार आयोजित छलफल कार्यक्रमलाई सम्बोधन गर्दै अध्यक्ष ओलीले यस्तो धारणा राखेका हुन्।

पार्टीको सङ्घर्षशील इतिहासबारे बोल्दै अध्यक्ष ओलीले भने, ‘एमाले कुनै अरूको सहारामा मात्र उभिने लहरो होइन, आफ्नै बलमा उम्रेको, हुर्केको र अनेकौं आँधी हुरी, तुफान तथा बाढीको सामना गरेर दह्रो बनेको एक स्वतन्त्र वृक्ष हो।’

छलफलका क्रममा उनले संसद्मा पार्टीको भूमिकालाई थप जनमुखी र प्रभावकारी बनाउनुपर्नेमा समेत जोड दिएका थिए।

articles.title: Elephant safaris at crossroads as Chitwan weighs ethical tourism shift
articles.summary:
On Friday afternoon, nature guide Samjhana Tiwari posted a video on Facebook showing a long queue of tourist vehicles heading towards the Baghmara Buffer Zone Community Forest for elephant and boat safaris.

“There are so many vehicles. You would not even see this many at a bus station,” Tiwari said in the video.

The footage came during the off-season, yet it showed a steady stream of visitors arriving for jungle activities in the forest area adjoining Sauraha, Nepal’s largest wildlife tourism hub. Tiwari had posted the video to draw attention to growing concerns over crowd management after seeing vehicles carrying tourists move directly towards elephant and boat boarding points.

But a Supreme Court order published just a day earlier had shifted the conversation in Sauraha from managing tourist crowds to questioning the future of one of Chitwan’s most recognisable attractions.

The court’s directive asking authorities to explore alternatives to elephant safaris has opened a debate among tourism entrepreneurs, conservationists, elephant owners, and local communities over whether traditional elephant rides can continue and how a transition to more ethical models could affect the local economy.

On September 14, 2021, animal rights advocates, including Sanjay Adhikari of the Forum for Protection of Public Interest (Pro Public), filed a writ petition at the Supreme Court seeking stronger legal protection for elephants. The petition called for an end to practices considered cruel to elephants, proper documentation of elephant ownership transfers, action against illegal trade, restrictions on prolonged chaining and a shift away from using elephants for rides, arguing that they should be used primarily for viewing.

The Supreme Court issued its verdict on December 17, 2025. The full text of the order, passed by a joint bench of Justices Hari Prasad Phuyal and Tek Prasad Dhungana, was published on the court’s website last Thursday.

The 62-point order includes several directives on elephant welfare, with one of its key provisions calling for alternatives to elephant safaris. The decision has since triggered a wider debate in Chitwan’s tourism sector about how to balance animal welfare with the economic importance of an activity that has supported local businesses for decades.

Point 48 of the order states that allowing tourists to ride elephants must be reconsidered from an animal welfare perspective and that alternative approaches should be adopted. At the same time, the court acknowledged the economic role of elephant safaris in generating income, promoting tourism and creating employment in places such as Sauraha.

For decades, elephant safaris have been among the main attractions for visitors to Chitwan National Park and its surrounding areas. Tourists, especially international visitors, have traditionally taken elephant rides to explore grasslands and forests to spot rhinos, deer, wild boars and other wildlife.

Tourism entrepreneurs say any transition away from elephant rides must be carefully planned, as thousands of people depend directly or indirectly on wildlife tourism.

“We cannot ignore animal welfare, but we also have to consider the livelihoods of people who depend on elephant safaris,” said a tourism entrepreneur in Sauraha. “The transition should be practical and involve all stakeholders.”

Conservationists, however, see the court order as an opportunity to redesign Chitwan’s wildlife tourism model.

They argue that alternatives such as jeep safaris, guided jungle walks, canoe trips and birdwatching tours can offer visitors rewarding wildlife experiences without relying on elephant rides.

“Tourism must evolve with changing global practices,” said a conservationist involved in wildlife protection. “The focus should be on observing animals in their natural habitat rather than using them as a means of transport.”

Elephant owners and mahouts, meanwhile, have raised concerns about what will happen to domesticated elephants if safari rides are discontinued. Many elephants currently used in tourism are maintained through income generated from safari operations.

Stakeholders say the government must prepare a transition plan covering elephant care, employment support and the development of alternative tourism products before introducing major changes.

The debate comes as Nepal’s wildlife tourism sector faces the challenge of balancing conservation priorities with economic realities. Chitwan National Park attracts hundreds of thousands of domestic and international visitors every year, and tourism remains a key source of income for communities surrounding the park.

Sauraha, located on the edge of Chitwan National Park, has long built its tourism economy around jungle activities, including elephant safaris. Local businesses fear that a sudden end to elephant rides without viable alternatives could affect hotels, guides, transport operators and communities dependent on tourist spending.

Environmental groups, however, argue that Nepal must gradually move away from tourism models that rely on animals for entertainment and align with growing international demand for ethical wildlife experiences.

As authorities and stakeholders begin discussions on implementing the court’s directive, the challenge for Chitwan will be finding a way to protect elephants while preserving the economic lifeline that wildlife tourism provides to local communities.

Point 48 of the court order states that “forcing a gradually disappearing species like the elephant to carry humans appears to be inherently irresponsible behaviour”. The court observed that an elephant’s spine, legs and body structure were not naturally designed to carry human weight. Carrying heavy loads for long periods and walking continuously, it said, can cause physical stress, including joint and leg problems.

“Thus, using elephants merely as tools for entertainment or tourism is incompatible with our obligation towards their value and welfare as living beings,” the order states.

In Point 51, the court suggested replacing traditional elephant safaris with alternatives such as “elephant walks” and “elephant bushwalks”.

“In accordance with welfare standards, it is essential to establish legal and policy frameworks to replace elephant safaris and cruel tethering systems in Nepal, transitioning towards an ethical and eco-friendly model,” the order states.

The court has also encouraged Nepal to adopt wildlife tourism practices used in other countries, including elephant-friendly walks and observing elephants from a safe distance without direct interaction.

But implementing such changes could have major economic consequences for communities around Chitwan National Park, where elephant safaris have long been a source of income.

The Baghmara Buffer Zone Community Forest, located on the outskirts of Sauraha, covers only 215 hectares. Yet at its peak, the forest generated around Rs30 million annually, according to former chairman Jitu Lama Tamang. Nearly one-third of that revenue came from elephant safaris.

Around seven or eight community forests surrounding Chitwan National Park rely heavily on elephant safaris for income. Elephant rides have not been allowed inside the national park for nearly 15 years. The activity is now limited to buffer zone community forests bordering the park.

Government-owned elephants are not used for tourist rides. The safaris are operated using privately owned domesticated elephants.

“Chinese tourists have a strong interest in elephant safaris. Even during the monsoon, when tourist arrivals usually decline, Chinese visitors have continued to arrive, and almost all of them take elephant rides. After safari income declined following Covid-19, Chinese tourists brought some hope,” said Bhuwaneshwar Prasad (BP) Chaudhary, chairman of Baghmara Buffer Zone Community Forest.

He warned that replacing elephant safaris without proper alternatives could significantly reduce the forest’s income.

However, Chaudhary also acknowledged that demand for elephant rides has been declining. In December 2014, Munich-based organisation Pro Wildlife had urged tourism operators to reduce activities involving elephant rides, arguing that such practices were inconsistent with modern wildlife tourism standards.

“European tourists generally do not ride elephants anymore. Nepali tourists may try it once but rarely repeat the experience. These days, Chinese tourists are the main group taking elephant rides,” Chaudhary said.

Former Baghmara chairman Tamang said local communities have also become increasingly concerned about keeping domesticated elephants near settlements. He said captive elephants often attract wild male elephants, increasing the risk of human-wildlife conflict.

“There were discussions about keeping domesticated elephants together on the edge of the forest rather than scattered around settlements. The government needed to provide land for that purpose. The Supreme Court order has also moved towards a sanctuary model,” Tamang said.

He said the time had come to ensure that tourism activities do not come at the cost of elephant welfare.

Most elephant safaris in Chitwan operate around Sauraha. The elephants involved are affiliated with the United Elephant Operation Cooperative Limited.

According to cooperative chairman Dipendra Khatiwada, the cooperative currently has 30 elephants, while another 14 operate independently. Around 38 to 40 elephants are used for safaris daily.

The cooperative was also named as a defendant in the writ petition filed at the Supreme Court.

Khatiwada said elephant safari operations had already declined significantly. Before the Covid-19 pandemic, the cooperative alone had around 63 elephants working in safaris. As tourism collapsed during the pandemic, some rented elephants were returned while others were sold to India.

“Everyone now agrees that the elephants that remain must be managed properly,” he said.

However, he said developing alternatives would require government support and clear policies.

“We have been asked to find alternatives to safaris, but this cannot be done through our efforts alone. How far will an ‘elephant walk’ extend? How will it operate? What policy framework supports it? The government must answer these questions,” Khatiwada said.

He said tourism stakeholders would respect the court order but cautioned against an abrupt transition.

“Replacing elephant safaris overnight could disrupt the entire tourism sector. We need enough time, clear policies and promotional campaigns to introduce new models properly,” he said.

Khatiwada also urged the government to address broader issues related to elephant management.

“The court has shown concern for the welfare of the elephants we rear. But it would have been better if it had also addressed issues such as the shortage of grazing land and difficulties in providing enough grass for elephants,” he said.

Tourism entrepreneur Hari Bhakta Ghimire said the government must introduce a clear policy following the court ruling.

Ghimire, who opened a hotel in Sauraha in 1982, introduced elephants for safari operations soon afterwards. He currently owns two adult elephants and a two-year-old calf.

He argued that elephant safaris have been closely linked with Chitwan’s tourism history and should not be viewed only from the perspective of animal welfare concerns.

“People in Nepal and India have used elephants for riding since ancient times. Elephant safaris in Chitwan began with the establishment of the national park. Tiger Tops, which opened in 1964, eight years before the park was established, also operated elephant safaris. It is a long-standing tradition,” Ghimire said.

He said tourism entrepreneurs had invested heavily in caring for domesticated elephants and that these realities should also have been considered.

Basu Dhungana, a conservationist and owner of a tourist resort in Kumroj near Sauraha, said the shift away from elephant rides is becoming inevitable as global tourism increasingly moves towards ethical wildlife experiences.

Dhungana, who opened his resort three years ago, does not offer elephant safaris. He said the government, community forests, hotels and tourism entrepreneurs should work together to develop genuinely elephant-friendly tourism models.

Bed Kumar Dhakal, spokesperson for the Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation, said elephant management was a serious issue for the department.

He said the government would work to implement the court’s directives while balancing them with the practical concerns of elephant owners.

Chitwan National Park remains Nepal’s most popular wildlife destination, attracting around 300,000 domestic and international visitors annually. Besides elephant safaris, the park offers jeep safaris, boat trips on rivers and streams bordering the park, and guided jungle walks.

The challenge now is to determine whether Chitwan can preserve its appeal as a wildlife destination while moving towards a tourism model that protects elephants and sustains the communities that have long depended on them.

articles.title: Voices of discontent continue to resonate at Maitighar
articles.summary:
The faces at Kathmandu's Maitighar Mandala change every day, but the message remains much the same.

On Saturday afternoon, exhausted doctors joined rape survivors, families of jailed Gen Z protesters and victims of alleged loan-sharking at Nepal's most visible protest ground, underscoring the growing disconnect between the government's promises and the grievances of ordinary citizens.

“We heal others. But who heals us?” Beneath that mask was an illustration of a face covered by another mask, which was labeled 'Doctor in distress,' showing tears streaming from the doctor's eyes.

They were intern doctors, medical officers and resident doctors from hospitals across Nepal.

Dr Krishna Sedhari, one of the protesters, said trainee doctors and medical officers were routinely made to work far beyond the limits set by Nepal's Labour Act, 2017.

“The law allows a maximum of 12 working hours a day, or 72 hours a week, with at least one mandatory day off,” he said. "But we are forced to work much longer than that. Doctors barely get any rest. That's why we've come to the streets."

Nearby, another young doctor, Pragyan Basnet, held up a placard that read: "A doctor who hasn't slept all night is sick. The healthcare system is sick. The country is sick."

“This isn't just about us,” Basnet said. “Poor people depend on hospitals like Bir Hospital and Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital. Why should doctors who have been awake for 26 straight hours be expected to treat patients? A doctor who has gone without sleep for 24 hours is no different from someone treating patients under the influence of alcohol.”

He said having a young prime minister, education minister and health minister meant little if the state remained unwilling to listen to young healthcare professionals.

“You cannot expect the country's healthcare system to improve while the doctors delivering those services continue to be overworked and exhausted,” he said. “The prime minister and ministers take weekends off. We don't even get a single day of rest.”

Only minutes earlier, at the gate of Singha Durbar, police had dragged away two women who had come hoping to meet Home Minister Sudan Gurung.

Binu Yadav and Niharika Rajput said they had spent the past five days trying to get the government to hear their grievances.

Standing outside the government complex, they rang handbells, the election symbol of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP).

“Maybe before they ignored us because they thought we belonged to another party,” Yadav said. "Now we're ringing the bell. Perhaps they’ll think we're RSP supporters. Will they listen now? During the election, they told us the bell symbol stood for justice and good governance. Today we're ringing that same bell to ask Rabi dai whether it will deliver justice for us.”

She said they had repeatedly been detained simply for demanding justice.

Rajput questioned whether citizens had to die before the state paid attention.

“Does everyone have to end up like Nirmala before they receive justice?” she asked, referring to the rape and murder of teenager Nirmala Panta, a case that remains unresolved years later. “Will they only wait outside our hospital beds after we’re dead, like they now say ‘Justice for Nirmala’ and ‘Justice for Ganesh’? If the government truly intends to deliver justice while we’re alive, then meet us now."

Rajput has spent years pursuing justice after alleging she was raped. Although a DNA test reportedly matched the accused, Shivraj Shrestha of Kshireshwornath Municipality-3 in Dhanusha district, she says she was later forced into a settlement after the District Court in Dhanusha acquitted him. She has since continued her battle for justice.

Yadav, too, says she is a survivor of violence.

While Yadav and Rajput rang bells outside Singha Durbar, another demonstration unfolded a short walk away at Maitighar.

Campaigners against caste discrimination held placards demanding an end to untouchability.

One asked simply: “Can't your conscience recognise another human being?”

Despite persistent monsoon rain, Maitighar Mandala hosted nine separate protests and sit-ins on Saturday alone.

Some protesters have lived there under makeshift tents for months.

Among them is 47-year-old Uma Khatri from Okhaldhunga.

For the past three months, she has slept under a plastic shelter demanding justice for her 23-year-old son, Milan Khatri.

He was shot twice by police during the Gen Z protests on September 8, 2025. Doctors initially said he was out of danger after emergency treatment.

As the number of gunshot victims at hospitals increased, doctors began asking some stable patients to return home to free up beds. Uma says her son Milan was discharged and was on his way towards Balkot on September 9 when he was seen in Maharajgunj amid the unrest.

She alleges that police later used a video showing him at the scene to file a murder case against him, even though he had only gone out while looking for a ride or vehicle. That day, Assistant Sub-Inspector Milan Rai and Police Constable Uttam Thapa were killed at the nearby Maharajgunj Police Circle.

“He was not even inside the police station. They watched a video and filed four or five cases against him,” Uma said.

Milan was arrested from Maitighar Mandala on October 26, 2025, and has remained in custody since then, according to Uma.

Uma, who survives by selling roasted corn on Kathmandu’s streets, has spent three months at Maitighar seeking justice from the Rastriya Swatantra Party-led government, which came to power on the back of the Gen Z protests in which her son was shot.

“The young people who took bullets helped bring these leaders to power,” she said. “But those same leaders haven’t even signed a single paper to help the youths who were injured.”

She said Milan had been the family's only hope.

“After he was jailed, our whole family fell apart.”

Uma says she has met Home Minister Sudan Gurung several times, including at Maitighar and Singha Durbar.

“He told us not to worry and said my son would be released,” she said.

“Nothing has happened. If my son had actually killed someone or committed a crime, we could accept that he was serving a sentence. But how can they keep an innocent person behind bars for so long?”

Amit Khanal “Urja” of the Gen Z Movement Alliance says the government appears more interested in addressing populist issues than confronting the everyday suffering of ordinary citizens.

He pointed to the government’s response to victims of loan-sharking as an example.

“The issue of loan-sharking victims was tied to the entire Madhes region. The government knew it could become politically difficult,” Khanal told Kantipur. “That is why the home minister himself travelled to Bara and held talks. But this government has not taken any decision in favour of the Gen Z protesters who suffered in the very movement that brought it to power.”

He said families of people detained for participating in the uprisings have been staging sit-ins for months, but the government has failed to address their demands.

“The government travelled to Bara and reached an agreement with loan-shark victims, but it has not even promised to investigate allegations of fraud involving the family of Nishan Mainali, whose family has been protesting at Maitighar,” he said. “The home minister may have met some victims, but the real question is whether those meetings have produced any solution.”

Among those still waiting for justice at Maitighar Mandala is 48-year-old Bhag Narayan Mandal from Barahathawa, Sarlahi.

He says his family was trapped by a predatory loan arrangement while he was working in Bahrain.

In 2015, his wife, Uma Mahato, borrowed Rs150,000 from the family of Nirmala Mainali. Ten days later, she was made to sign a promissory document stating a debt of Rs1 million.

“They did not just take our money. Later, while I was still abroad, they took our 10 kattha of land (one kattha equals 0.03386 hectare) as well,” Mandal said. “We staged protests in the district first. When we heard that justice could be found at Maitighar, we came here. It has now been 105 days.”

According to Mandal, his brother-in-law transferred 10 kattha of land to his wife Uma’s name in 2017. He alleges that Nirmala repeatedly pressured her to mortgage the land.

“Uma did not know how mortgage arrangements worked,” he said. “She was told that her son Nishan would handle the paperwork.”

Mandal says Nishan took her through the ward office and eventually to the land revenue office. As Uma could not read or write, she signed whatever documents she was instructed to sign.

“We kept paying money, but the loan never ended,” Mandal said. “It was only in 2022, when our daughter was getting married, that we discovered the mortgaged land had already been transferred to Nirmala Mainali’s name.”

He said he was working as a cleaner in Bahrain when his wife informed him of the transfer.

“I felt as if the ground had disappeared beneath my feet,” he said.

The family also filed a complaint at the chief district officer’s office, but Mandal says the decision went against them.

A decision document obtained by Kantipur from the District Administration Office states that Uma Kumari had voluntarily executed a land transfer agreement and received agricultural rights over the property.

“Therefore, as the transaction appears to be a transfer of land ownership rather than a case of predatory lending or a loan transaction, further investigation and action under the loan-sharking complaint process is not required,” the decision stated.

Mandal and his wife had been staying at Maitighar for the protest. But Uma has since fallen ill due to the cold weather and is recovering in a rented room.

“She developed fever, diarrhoea and vomiting. Our son took her to the hospital, and she is now resting in his rented room,” Mandal said.

Maitighar Mandala has become a gathering point for people with a wide range of grievances, from road accident victims to supporters of the former monarchy.

Victims of loan sharking from Madhes also marched to Kathmandu demanding justice. After beginning a Janakpur-Kathmandu foot march on June 29, they were met by Home Minister Sudan Gurung in Nijgadh, Bara. Talks followed, and the government reached a nine-point agreement with them.

But many others protesting with different demands are still waiting for relief.

Despite the Rastriya Swatantra Party-led government coming to power on the promise of change and holding a near two-thirds majority in Parliament, the number of people taking to the streets seeking justice has continued to rise.

According to data from the Kathmandu Valley Police Office, Ranipokhari, more than 800 protests and sit-ins were recorded in Kathmandu alone after Balendra Shah became prime minister.

The figures show 120 protests during the period between mid-March and mid-April, 222 between mid-April and mid-May, 240 between mid-May and mid-June and 282 between mid-June and mid-July. A total of 1,771 protests were recorded in the current fiscal year.

In comparison, Kathmandu Valley recorded 2,145 protests in the previous fiscal year and 2,252 in 2023/24, according to police data.

Among those protesting at Maitighar is Laxmi Singh from Jajarkot, who suffers from kidney disease.

“I am a single woman and both my kidneys are damaged,” she said. “I need support for treatment. The government must be responsible and accountable for ensuring healthcare for its citizens.”

She has been staying at Maitighar while collecting financial support and has demanded free treatment for patients like her.

Not every demand raised at Maitighar carries the same weight.

Ganesh Giri Yogi, another protester at the site, has been demanding that Nepal should have a yogi as prime minister, claiming he himself is the right candidate.

“From now on, the country should be run according to Sanatan values, and a yogi should become prime minister. People across the country need to awaken,” he said.

People protesting around Maitighar, and even some police officers deployed there for security, jokingly address him as “Prime Minister.”

For years, Maitighar has served as Nepal’s most visible protest ground. But the growing number of unresolved grievances there reflects a broader challenge for a government that came to power promising to address public anger and demands for change.

articles.title: Helicopter rescues offer lifeline to teenage mothers in Nepal’s remote hills
articles.summary:
For 19-year-old Sushila Roka of ward 14 in Musikot Municipality, Rukum West, the morning of June 4 became the most difficult day of her life. Her family had been preparing to welcome her first child. But as her labour pains intensified, excitement quickly turned into fear. Sushila, who became pregnant at a young age, developed serious complications.

Her family rushed her to the district hospital, but doctors delivered devastating news.

“Forget about saving the baby. You did not bring her in on time, and we cannot save it,” Sushila’s sister-in-law, Nandakala Roka, recalled doctors telling them.

“The whole family was devastated after hearing that.”

Sushila was carrying twins. Although her family rushed her to the hospital, hoping both babies could be saved, doctors warned them of the risks. After a prolonged effort, doctors delivered one baby without surgery, but had to perform a caesarean section to deliver the second.

But the danger was not over.

Sushila suffered severe bleeding after delivery. Doctors advised that she be transferred to the provincial hospital in Surkhet. She was airlifted by a Nepali Army helicopter after the District Administration Office, Rukum West, issued a recommendation for emergency evacuation.

Only then did the family regain hope.

A similar ordeal unfolded for 15-year-old Karuna Bista of ward 2 in Jagannath Rural Municipality, Bajura. She gave birth while unconscious on November 27 last year.

Karuna became pregnant during adolescence and lost consciousness after sudden labour pains before the baby was delivered. By the time she reached the district hospital, her condition had become critical.

The doctors suggested she needed treatment outside the district due to excessive bleeding and delivery complications.

“My daughter-in-law fainted while giving birth, perhaps because she was too young,” said Karuna’s mother-in-law, Amrita Bista. “My grandson was born while she was unconscious.”

Although the baby survived, Karuna didn’t regain consciousness for two days. She was later airlifted to the provincial hospital for further treatment.

Nilima Sherpa, 15, from ward 2 of Makalu Rural Municipality in Sankhuwasabha, faced a similar crisis.

She became pregnant at 15 and was flown by a Nepali Army helicopter to Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital in Kathmandu on March 22 after suffering severe bleeding.

Nilima said she entered pregnancy with little knowledge of childbirth, potential complications or the preparations needed to deal with the risks, as she was still only 15 years old.

“I was not thinking about how I would deliver the baby. I was constantly afraid that I might not survive,” she said. “Becoming a mother for the first time was the most terrifying experience of my life.”

She said timely coordination among relatives, local authorities and concerned agencies, followed by helicopter evacuation, gave her a second chance at life.

“I never imagined a helicopter would come for the rescue and that all three lives would be saved,” Nandakala said. “The timely evacuation saved the mother and the babies.”

Because Sushila gave birth to twins at a young age, both babies have very low birth weights. Doctors say they need to remain in the hospital for at least another month.

Nandakala said Sushila’s health remains weak, and she cannot breastfeed directly. The milk has to be expressed and fed to the babies through a syringe.

Amrita in Bajura had a similar experience.

“My daughter-in-law regained consciousness only two days after reaching the hospital,” she said.

She said the free emergency evacuation service was the only reason Karuna reached the hospital in time.

Doctors say emergency referrals from remote districts remain necessary because many local hospitals lack specialised facilities.

Sijan Rawal, a doctor at Dolpa District Hospital, said even after a successful delivery, patients often have to be referred to better-equipped hospitals to save the newborns.

“We do not have paediatric specialists, essential equipment or enough medical staff,” he said. “Referring patients is sometimes the only option to save their lives.”

Nilima also credits the air rescue for saving her life.

“I received treatment on time because of everyone’s support, and both my baby and I are safe,” she said.

She said becoming a mother at such a young age had affected her both physically and mentally.

“My health has improved, but any sign of bleeding still frightens me. Although my body has recovered, I have not fully overcome the fear of going through it again,” she said.

In Nepal’s remote mountain communities, reaching health facilities remains a major challenge. Difficult terrain and hours-long travel often force women to give birth at home, increasing the risks, doctors say.

To address such emergencies, the government has been running the President Women Upliftment Programme since the fiscal year 2018-19. The programme provides emergency helicopter evacuation for pregnant women and new mothers facing life-threatening complications in remote areas.

The service is used for cases involving complicated pregnancies, severe bleeding or situations where delays in reaching healthcare facilities could put lives at risk.

Based on recommendations from chief district officers and local health institutions, the Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, and Social Security mobilises the Nepali Army for rescue operations.

Helicopters stationed at the Central Air Base in Kathmandu and the Western Air Base Wing in Surkhet have been used to evacuate women from designated local levels across all seven provinces.

Brigadier General Raja Ram Basnet, spokesperson for the Army, said the emergency maternity evacuation programme has become a lifesaving service for mothers and newborns.

According to him, the free helicopter rescue service is available across all local levels in 19 districts: Taplejung, Sankhuwasabha, Bhojpur, Khotang, Solukhumbu, Okhaldhunga, Manang, Mustang, Rukum East, Rukum West, Jajarkot, Dolpa, Kalikot, Mugu, Humla, Bajhang, Bajura, Achham and Darchula.

The programme is partially available in remote areas of 25 other districts, where women facing life-threatening pregnancy or childbirth complications are evacuated to suitable hospitals.

So far, around 950 pregnant women and new mothers have been rescued by helicopter under the programme across the country. Data provided by the Nepali Army shows that 19 percent of those rescued were teenage mothers.

Dr Lalit Jung Shahi, an obstetrician and gynaecologist at Karnali Provincial Hospital, said young mothers often require surgical intervention due to pregnancy-related risks.

“Pregnant teenagers face a higher risk of high blood pressure. Because of that, it is often impossible to complete delivery without surgery,” he said.

“Teenage mothers brought in through helicopter rescue often face excessive bleeding after labour begins, low birth weight babies, severe haemorrhage and anaemia.”

Anju Dhungana, chief of the Women Empowerment Division at the Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, and Social Security, said all three tiers of government must step up efforts to curb child marriage and prevent girls from becoming mothers too early.

articles.title: कपिलवस्तुमा दुई वर्षभन्दा पुराना सबै मुद्दा फर्छ्योट, एक वर्षमा ६२ प्रतिशत मुद्दा किनारा
articles.summary:
जेन्जी आन्दोलनका क्रममा अदालतमा भएको आगजनी तथा निर्वाचनको बीचमा पनि कपिलवस्तु जिल्ला अदालतले ऐतिहासिक उपलब्धि हासिल गरेको छ। अदालतमा वर्षौंदेखि विचाराधीन रहेका दुई वर्षभन्दा पुराना सबै मुद्दा फर्छ्योट गर्न सफल भएको हो।

गत आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ मा दुई वर्षभन्दा पुराना २ सय ७८ वटा सबै मुद्दा फर्छ्योट गरिएको अदालतको वार्षिक प्रतिवेदनमा उल्लेख छ।

अदालतका श्रेस्तेदार अनन्त मरासिनीले लामो समयदेखि विचाराधीन रहेका दुई वर्षभन्दा पुराना सबै मुद्दा फर्छ्योट हुनु अदालत स्थापनाकालदेखि हालसम्मकै ऐतिहासिक उपलब्धि भएको बताए। उनका अनुसार न्यायाधीश तथा कर्मचारीहरूको सामूहिक प्रयासबाट यो उपलब्धि हासिल भएको हो।

भदौ २३ र २४ गते जेन्जी आन्दोलनका क्रममा अदालतमा आगजनी हुँदा श्रेस्ता तथा अभिलेख (रेकर्ड) मा ठूलो क्षति पुगेको थियो। त्यसका कारण दुई महिनाभन्दा बढी समय अदालतको कामकाज प्रायः ठप्प बनेको थियो। यस्तै, गत फागुन २१ गते भएको निर्वाचनका क्रममा न्यायाधीश तथा कर्मचारीको सरुवाका कारण पनि अदालतको काम प्रभावित भएको थियो।

गत आर्थिक वर्षमा अदालतले कुल मुद्दामध्ये ६२ दशमलव ३४ प्रतिशत मुद्दा फर्छ्योट गरेको छ। अघिल्लो आर्थिक वर्षबाट जिम्मेवारी सरेर आएका १ हजार ५०९ र गत आर्थिक वर्षमा नयाँ दर्ता भएका २ हजार ३४२ गरी कुल ३ हजार ८५१ मुद्दामध्ये २ हजार ४०१ वटा मुद्दा फर्छ्योट भएका छन्। हाल १ हजार ४५० मुद्दा फर्छ्योट हुन बाँकी रहेका छन्।

आर्थिक वर्ष २०८१/८२ मा भने कुल मुद्दामध्ये ६५ दशमलव ८२ प्रतिशत मुद्दा फर्छ्योट गरिएको थियो। त्यस वर्ष जिम्मेवारी सरेर आएका र नयाँ दर्ता भएका गरी कुल ४ हजार ४१६ मुद्दा रहेका थिए।

गत आर्थिक वर्षमा देवानीतर्फ २ हजार ६४८, फौजदारीतर्फ १ हजार १५५, बन्दी प्रत्यक्षीकरणका ४ तथा निषेधाज्ञासम्बन्धी ४४ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका थिए।

हाल फर्छ्योट हुन बाँकी रहेका मुद्दामध्ये ६ महिनाभित्रका १ हजार ४७, ६ महिनादेखि एक वर्षसम्मका १९०, १२ देखि १८ महिनासम्मका १८० तथा १८ महिनादेखि दुई वर्षभित्रका ३३ मुद्दा रहेका छन्।

कपिलवस्तु जिल्ला अदालतमा हाल पाँच जना न्यायाधीशले मुद्दाको सुनुवाइ तथा फैसला गर्दै आएका छन्।

articles.title: विश्वकप फाइनलको ‘हाफ-टाइम’ मा बीटीएस र साकिराले साङ्गीतिक प्रस्तुति दिने
articles.summary:
फिफा विश्वकपको इतिहासमै पहिलो पटक फाइनल खेलको मध्यान्तरमा साङ्गीतिक प्रस्तुति समावेश गरिने भएको छ।

स्पेन र अर्जेन्टिनाबीच अमेरिकाको न्युजर्सीस्थित मेटलाइफ स्टेडियममा हुने फाइनल खेलको हाफ-टाइममा मडोना, साकिरा, बीटीएस र जस्टिन बिबर जस्ता विश्वप्रसिद्ध कलाकारहरूले प्रस्तुति दिने तय भएको छ।

यस नयाँ शैलीले खेल जगत्मा भने विवाद निम्त्याएको छ। साङ्गीतिक प्रस्तुतिका कारण मध्यान्तरको समय २५ मिनेटसम्म लम्बिनेछ। जबकी अन्तर्राष्ट्रिय फुटबल एसोसिएसन बोर्ड (आईएफएबी) को नियमअनुसार खेलाडीहरूले बढीमा १५ मिनेट मात्र विश्राम पाउनुपर्ने व्यवस्था छ।

लामो विश्रामले खेलाडीहरूको शारीरिक निष्क्रियता बढाउने र चोटपटकको जोखिम निम्त्याउने भन्दै चिन्ता व्यक्त गरिएको छ।

फिफाले यसलाई खेलकुद र सङ्गीतको ऐतिहासिक सङ्गम भनेको छ। लाइभ नेसनका जेम्स म्यासिङले खेलकुदलाई चलचित्र, नाटक वा म्युजियम जस्ता अन्य मनोरञ्जनका विधासँग प्रतिस्पर्धा गर्न साङ्गीतिक प्रस्तुति आवश्यक रहेको तर्क गरेका छन्।

तर, खेल विश्लेषक र फुटबल प्रशंसकहरूले भने फुटबलको मौलिकता हराउने र खेलाडीको सुरक्षा खतरामा पर्ने भन्दै यसको विरोध गरेका छन्।

ब्रिटिश फुटबल सामग्री निर्माता एलिस प्लेटनले भने, ‘विश्वकप फाइनल आफैंमा ऐतिहासिक र सबैभन्दा बढी हेरिने खेल हो, यसलाई थप आकर्षक बनाउन यस्ता कृत्रिम शोहरूको आवश्यकता पर्दैन।’

अमेरिकी खेलकुदमा हाफ-टाइम शो निकै लोकप्रिय रहे पनि युरोप र अन्य क्षेत्रमा यसको स्वीकार्यता सुस्त छ। यसअघि क्लब विश्वकपमा पनि २४ मिनेटको मध्यान्तर गरी कोल्डप्ले जस्ता ब्यान्डले प्रस्तुति दिएका थिए।

आलोचकहरूले भने फिफाको यस व्यावसायिक कदमले आगामी दिनमा घरेलु लिगहरूमा पनि खेलाडीको हित विपरीत यस्ता लामो शोहरू भित्रिन सक्ने डर व्यक्त गरेका छन्।

articles.title: राति १० बजेपछि नारायणगढ–मुग्लिन सडकमा आवागमन बन्द
articles.summary:
स्थानीय प्रशासनले नारायणगढ-मुग्लिन सडक र चितवनतर्फको पृथ्वी राजमार्ग आज राति १० बजेदेखि बन्द गर्ने भएको छ।

जिल्लाका विभिन्न स्थानहरुसहित धादिङलगायत जिल्लामा पहिरोको जोखिम भएकाले नारायणगढ-मुग्लिन-काठमाडौं सडक राति १० बजेपछि बन्द रहने जनाएको छ।

प्रमुख जिल्ला अधिकारी गणेश अर्यालद्वारा जारी सूचनामा रातको समयमा सवारी सञ्चालन राखिरहँदा हुन सक्ने जोखिमलाई मध्यनजर गर्दै सवारी बन्द गरिएको उल्लेख छ।

रातिमा सवारीसाधन र यात्रा गर्दा स्थानीय प्रशासन र सरोकारवाला सुरक्षा निकायसँग समन्वय गरी मात्रै गर्न सूचनामा अनुरोध गरिएको छ।

वर्षातका कारण शनिबार रातिसमेत यो सडक बन्द गरिएको थियो।

articles.title: सडकको अवस्था बुझ्न कर्णालीमा पूर्वाधार विकास मन्त्री लम्साल
articles.summary:
कर्णालीका सडकको वास्तविक अवस्था कागजी प्रतिवेदनबाट होइन, स्थलमै पुगेर बुझ्ने उद्देश्यसहित पूर्वाधार विकास मन्त्री सुनिल लम्साल आइतबार जुम्ला आइपुगे। बर्खाका कारण पहिरो, हिलो र अवरुद्ध सडक हुँदै यात्रा गर्दै उनले कर्णाली राजमार्ग, नाग्म–गमगढी सडक र डोल्पा जोड्ने सडकको स्थलगत अनुगमन गरे।

अनुगमनका क्रममा उनले सडक निर्माणको प्रगति, बजेट कार्यान्वयन, स्थानीयका गुनासा तथा वर्षौंदेखि अलपत्र परेका पूर्वाधार आयोजनाको अवस्थाबारे प्रत्यक्ष जानकारी लिए।

पर्यटकीय क्षेत्र जुम्लाको गुठीचौर पाटन पुगेर मन्त्री लम्सालले गोठालासँग भेटघाट गरे। गोठालाहरूले पाटनसम्म पुग्ने सडक पक्की बनाइदिन आग्रह गरेपछि उनले आवश्यक पहल गर्ने आश्वासन दिए। गुठीचौरलाई व्यवस्थित पूर्वाधारसँग जोड्न सके कर्णालीकै प्रमुख पर्यटकीय गन्तव्यका रूपमा विकास गर्न सकिने उनको भनाइ थियो। पर्यटन र पूर्वाधारलाई सँगसँगै अघि बढाउनुपर्ने आवश्यकता उनले औँल्याए। हाल उक्त पाटनमा हरेक वर्ष हजारौं पर्यटक पुग्ने गरेका छन्।

अनुगमनका क्रममा मन्त्री लम्सालले जुम्लामा वर्षौंदेखि निर्माण सम्पन्न हुन नसकेका तथा अलपत्र अवस्थामा रहेका भौतिक संरचनाको समेत अवलोकन गरे। उनले कर्णालीका सबै जिल्लाका सडक आयोजनाको अवस्था बुझ्न स्थलगत भ्रमणमा निस्किएको स्पष्ट पारे।

‘कर्णालीका सबै जिल्लाका सडकको अनुगमन गरिरहेका छौं। सबै सडकमा बजेट विनियोजन गरिएको छ। हामीले छुट्याएको बजेट पर्याप्त भयो कि भएन, थप बजेट आवश्यक छ कि छैन भन्ने बुझ्न कर्णालीका जिल्लामा आएका हौं,’ मन्त्री लम्सालले भने। उनका अनुसार अहिलेको अनुगमनको उद्देश्य चुनौती पहिचान गर्दै आगामी वर्षका योजना अझ प्रभावकारी बनाउनु हो।

जुम्ला भ्रमणका क्रममा मन्त्री लम्सालले यसअघि खारेज भएको संघीय खानेपानी कार्यालय पुनः स्थापना गरिने प्रतिबद्धता पनि जनाए। ‘संघीय खानेपानी कार्यालय स्वीकृत भइसकेको छ। केही दिनमै काम सुरु हुन्छ,’ उनले भने।

२०८१ चैत ११ गतेको निर्णयअनुसार २०८२ साउन १ गतेदेखि जुम्लासहित अन्य १५ वटा अस्थायी संघीय खानेपानी कार्यालय खारेज गर्ने निर्णय गरिएको थियो। जुम्लासहित साविक कर्णालीका कालीकोट, मुगु र हुम्ला गरी चार जिल्लालाई कार्यक्षेत्र बनाएको उक्त कार्यालय जुम्लाबाट हटाइएको थियो।

बर्खाकै समयमा कर्णालीको भ्रमण गर्नु उपयुक्त निर्णय भएको उल्लेख गर्दै मन्त्री लम्सालले सडकको वास्तविक अवस्था प्रत्यक्ष रूपमा अनुभव गर्न पाएको बताए। ‘बर्खामै आइयो, एकदम ठीक भयो। सडक हेर्दै कर्णालीको सास्ती पनि भोगियो। अब योजना तर्जुमा गर्न सहज हुनेछ,’ उनले भने।

जुम्लामा रहँदा उनले आफ्नो मन्त्रालयअन्तर्गतका कार्यालयहरूको अवस्था अवलोकन गर्नुका साथै सेवाग्राहीका समस्या पनि सुने। अनुगमन टोलीमा मन्त्री लम्सालसँगै सांसद रमेशकुमार सापकोटा र सुशान्त वैदिक सहभागी थिए।

स्थानीयवासीले कर्णाली राजमार्गको स्तरोन्नति गर्न माग गर्दै मन्त्री लम्साललाई स्याउको माला लगाएर स्वागत गरेका थिए। वर्षायाममा निरन्तर पहिरो जाँदा राजमार्ग पटक–पटक अवरुद्ध हुने, त्यसले जुम्लाको मुख्य नगदे बाली स्याउको ढुवानी तथा निर्यातमा गम्भीर असर पार्ने गरेको भन्दै उनीहरूले दुई लेनको पक्की सडक निर्माण गर्न आग्रह गरे।

मन्त्री लम्सालले आइतबार कर्णालीको प्रसिद्ध चन्दननाथ मन्दिरमा दर्शन गर्नुका साथै कर्णाली स्वास्थ्य विज्ञान प्रतिष्ठानको अवलोकन गरेपछि मुगुतर्फ प्रस्थान गरेका छन्।

मन्त्री लम्साल शुक्रबारदेखि कर्णालीका प्रमुख राजमार्गहरूको स्थलगत अनुगमनमा छन्। केही साताअघि मात्रै उनले तीन वर्षभित्र कर्णालीका जिल्ला तथा स्थानीय तह जोड्ने मुख्य सडकलाई डबल लेनमा विस्तार गर्ने घोषणा गरेका थिए। सोही घोषणाको कार्यान्वयन अवस्था बुझ्न उनी सुर्खेतदेखि हुम्लासम्मका सडक आयोजनाको निरीक्षणमा निस्किएका हुन्।

उनको भ्रमण कर्णाली राजमार्गअन्तर्गत सुर्खेत–दैलेख–कालीकोट सडक खण्डको निरीक्षणबाट सुरु भएको हो। त्यसपछि कालीकोट हुँदै जुम्ला–कालीकोट सीमास्थित नाग्मसम्म पुगेर नाग्म–गमगढी सडकको निरीक्षण, स्थलमार्गबाट बाजुरा र त्यहाँबाट हवाईमार्ग हुँदै हुम्ला पुगेर सडक आयोजनाको अवस्था बुझ्ने कार्यक्रम तय गरिएको छ।

गत असार ४ गते प्रतिनिधिसभामा मन्त्री लम्सालले कर्णालीका मुख्य सडक तीन वर्षभित्र डबल लेनमा विस्तार गरिने घोषणा गरेका थिए। सडकका खाल्डाखुल्डी अब टालटुले शैलीमा नभई नियमित मर्मत प्रणालीमार्फत व्यवस्थापन गरिने पनि उनले बताएका थिए। सोही प्रतिबद्धताको कार्यान्वयन अवस्था बुझ्न उनी स्थलगत अनुगमनमा निस्किएको बताइएको छ।

कर्णालीका अधिकांश सडक अझै पनि जीर्ण अवस्थामै छन्। वर्षायाममा पहिरो र हिउँदमा धुलोका कारण स्थानीयले वर्षौंदेखि सास्ती खेप्दै आएका छन्। यही कारण कर्णाली राजमार्गलाई लामो समयदेखि ‘मृत्युमार्ग’को संज्ञा दिइँदै आएको चन्दननाथ नगरपालिका–४ का बालाराम नेपाली बताउँछन्।

सुर्खेतदेखि जुम्लासम्म फैलिएको २ सय ३२ किलोमिटर लामो कर्णाली राजमार्गमध्ये १ सय ३२ किलोमिटर सडक सडक डिभिजन कार्यालय सुर्खेत र १ सय किलोमिटर सडक सडक डिभिजन कार्यालय जुम्लाको कार्यक्षेत्रमा पर्छ।

नाग्मदेखि मुगुको सदरमुकाम गमगढीसम्मको ९३ किलोमिटर सडकमा नियमित सवारी सञ्चालन भइरहेको छ। गमगढीदेखि उत्तरी चिनियाँ नाका नाक्चेनाग्लासम्म प्रस्तावित ९३ किलोमिटर सडकमध्ये १८ किलोमिटर ट्र्याक खुलिसकेको छ भने बाँकी खण्डको विस्तृत परियोजना प्रतिवेदन (डीपीआर) तयार भइसकेको छ।

सडक डिभिजन कार्यालय जुम्लाका सूचना अधिकारी इन्जिनियर प्रदीप नारायण चौधरीका अनुसार सडकलाई विभिन्न खण्डमा विभाजन गरी निर्माण प्रक्रिया अघि बढाइएको छ।

articles.title: कपिलवस्तुमा दुई वर्षभन्दा पुराना सबै मुद्दा फर्छ्योट, एक वर्षमा ६२ प्रतिशत मुद्दा किनारा
articles.summary:
जेन्जी आन्दोलनका क्रममा अदालतमा भएको आगजनी तथा निर्वाचनको बीचमा पनि कपिलवस्तु जिल्ला अदालतले ऐतिहासिक उपलब्धि हासिल गरेको छ। अदालतमा वर्षौंदेखि विचाराधीन रहेका दुई वर्षभन्दा पुराना सबै मुद्दा फर्छ्योट गर्न सफल भएको हो।

गत आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ मा दुई वर्षभन्दा पुराना २ सय ७८ वटा सबै मुद्दा फर्छ्योट गरिएको अदालतको वार्षिक प्रतिवेदनमा उल्लेख छ।

अदालतका श्रेस्तेदार अनन्त मरासिनीले लामो समयदेखि विचाराधीन रहेका दुई वर्षभन्दा पुराना सबै मुद्दा फर्छ्योट हुनु अदालत स्थापनाकालदेखि हालसम्मकै ऐतिहासिक उपलब्धि भएको बताए। उनका अनुसार न्यायाधीश तथा कर्मचारीहरूको सामूहिक प्रयासबाट यो उपलब्धि हासिल भएको हो।

भदौ २३ र २४ गते जेन्जी आन्दोलनका क्रममा अदालतमा आगजनी हुँदा श्रेस्ता तथा अभिलेख (रेकर्ड) मा ठूलो क्षति पुगेको थियो। त्यसका कारण दुई महिनाभन्दा बढी समय अदालतको कामकाज प्रायः ठप्प बनेको थियो। यस्तै, गत फागुन २१ गते भएको निर्वाचनका क्रममा न्यायाधीश तथा कर्मचारीको सरुवाका कारण पनि अदालतको काम प्रभावित भएको थियो।

गत आर्थिक वर्षमा अदालतले कुल मुद्दामध्ये ६२ दशमलव ३४ प्रतिशत मुद्दा फर्छ्योट गरेको छ। अघिल्लो आर्थिक वर्षबाट जिम्मेवारी सरेर आएका १ हजार ५०९ र गत आर्थिक वर्षमा नयाँ दर्ता भएका २ हजार ३४२ गरी कुल ३ हजार ८५१ मुद्दामध्ये २ हजार ४०१ वटा मुद्दा फर्छ्योट भएका छन्। हाल १ हजार ४५० मुद्दा फर्छ्योट हुन बाँकी रहेका छन्।

आर्थिक वर्ष २०८१/८२ मा भने कुल मुद्दामध्ये ६५ दशमलव ८२ प्रतिशत मुद्दा फर्छ्योट गरिएको थियो। त्यस वर्ष जिम्मेवारी सरेर आएका र नयाँ दर्ता भएका गरी कुल ४ हजार ४१६ मुद्दा रहेका थिए।

गत आर्थिक वर्षमा देवानीतर्फ २ हजार ६४८, फौजदारीतर्फ १ हजार १५५, बन्दी प्रत्यक्षीकरणका ४ तथा निषेधाज्ञासम्बन्धी ४४ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका थिए।

हाल फर्छ्योट हुन बाँकी रहेका मुद्दामध्ये ६ महिनाभित्रका १ हजार ४७, ६ महिनादेखि एक वर्षसम्मका १९०, १२ देखि १८ महिनासम्मका १८० तथा १८ महिनादेखि दुई वर्षभित्रका ३३ मुद्दा रहेका छन्।

कपिलवस्तु जिल्ला अदालतमा हाल पाँच जना न्यायाधीशले मुद्दाको सुनुवाइ तथा फैसला गर्दै आएका छन्।

articles.title: The state resorted to physical violence to silence us
articles.summary:
Majid Ansari is a law student and legal activist who has been actively advocating for the constitutional rights of evicted squatter settlers. His advocacy led to the registration of a Supreme Court writ petition 082-WO-1237 challenging the government’s management of displaced families. On July 11, following heavy inundation at a holding centre in Kirtipur, Ansari and his fellow activists visited the site to observe the relocation of the settlers, only to face immediate resistance from state authorities.

The situation rapidly escalated when Ansari questioned the presence of unofficial actors commanding police personnel. He was subsequently subjected to a brutal physical assault by a group of police officers, leading to temporary unconsciousness and severe facial trauma. Following a chaotic detention process, extrajudicial surveillance at the hospital, and a wave of online hostility, Ansari remains steadfast in his pursuit of accountability. In his first interview since the incident, Ansari sat down with The Post’s Biken K Dawadi, detailing the events surrounding his violent arrest, the systemic failures within the security apparatus, and his refusal to be silenced by state-sponsored intimidation.

Why did you visit the holding centre for evicted squatter settlers in Kirtipur on July 11?

Heavy rainfall on the previous night caused inundation of the holding centre, displacing the evicted squatter families. News media had been broadcasting alarming updates regarding the crisis. My peers Monika Niraula, Sarishma Thapa, Riyab Baniya, and I visited the centre to observe the relocation of the evicted settlers as we felt a moral obligation to witness the situation firsthand. We arrived at the holding centre at around 4:30 PM to see how state authorities were managing the vulnerable citizens.

What initial obstacles did you encounter when you tried to gain access to the holding facility?

The police personnel stationed at the entrance blocked our path immediately and refused to grant us entry. We attempted to communicate politely with the officers, explaining our identity as law students who merely wished to observe. Our requests were met with complete defiance. While we were standing outside the gates, Sarishma noticed a fellow Gen Z activist, Ojaswi Thapa, inside the facility. He was giving commands to the police officers, and the security personnel were obeying his instructions. Sarishma immediately objected to his unclear administrative role. She asked the police officers about his legal capacity and demanded to know why he was permitted inside to command state forces while others were barred from entry.

How did the police officers react?

The police officers refused to provide a transparent answer. Instead, they told us that if we required such specific information, we must file a formal application with the information officer at the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers. It seemed like an attempt to evade accountability through bureaucratic stalling. I stated that an exhaustive formal process was completely unnecessary for such a query. I argued that if Ojaswi possessed a legitimate identity card which proved his official capacity, he should simply display it. I questioned the presence of unofficial actors inside a restricted state facility. This legal argument made the police officers visibly angry. Their demeanour transformed from indifference into hostility.

What specific actions were taking place concerning the squatter families?

To prevent further escalation, we dropped the dispute. We exited the main gate and walked towards the public pavement. From that vantage point, we observed that the displaced families were actively moving their meagre belongings under the supervision of the authorities. There were two passenger buses and a small cargo truck parked in a state of readiness. One bus had already been filled with people and was departing the scene. The other one remained stationary. The driver of the second bus was asking the police officers repeatedly whether their destination was Bode or Kharipati. The entire operation was marred by confusion. The police officers lacked consensus and clarity regarding the final destination. Some officers told the driver they were going to Bode, while others insisted they were heading to Kharipati. The displaced families looked visibly panicked because they had no official information regarding where their children and their belongings were being transported. Seeing their deep distress, we approached the police once again. We requested that they provide information to the families to alleviate their terror. The police dismissed our concerns and ordered us to stop playing politics, get away from the scene, and go back to our studies.

What happened next?

Following this exchange, Sarishma and I decided to board the second bus. We advised the families to remain peaceful and resilient while fighting for their constitutional rights. Suddenly, a policeman wearing a medical mask boarded the bus and addressed us with contempt. He stated mockingly that we did not look educated. He asked why we were lecturing others and told us to go study instead.

Could you describe the interaction you had with Ojaswi Thapa just before the violence erupted?

Approximately five minutes before the physical violence commenced, Ojaswi called me aside. I had become acquainted with him previously during various social movements and public campaigns. He looked at me directly and asked whether I maintained my trust in him. I responded by highlighting the uncertainty surrounding the squatter families. I requested him to use his influence to ensure their proper, timely management and to treat them with basic human dignity. He did not offer a detailed reply. Instead, he walked a short distance towards a group of police officers. I observed him leaning in close to whisper something directly to a police official.

What happened immediately after that whispered conversation?

Within a few minutes of that whispered conversation, the police forces formed an aggressive cordon around us, cutting off all exits. I saw several police officers roughing up Sarishma, treating her with disrespect. My immediate instinct was to shield her from their aggression. I did not raise my hands against any officer, nor did I engage in any form of physical retaliation. I resisted purely through verbal protest. Video evidence captured by onlookers clearly demonstrates that I kept one of my hands buried inside my pant pocket during the initial encounter. Suddenly, an officer shoved me violently from behind. I had seen them making suspicious hand gestures earlier, but I had not realised their violent intent.

How did the situation escalate into a physical assault?

When the officer shoved me from behind, I spun around and demanded to know who had committed that act. At that exact moment, Sarishma wrapped her arms around my torso to protect me. But the police forces had already decided to unleash physical violence. A group of twelve to fifteen police officers descended upon me simultaneously. They swarmed us from every angle, rendering us entirely helpless. The same masked policeman who had insulted our education on the bus lunged forward aggressively. He began punching me with his fists and striking my body with his boots. Four to five officers started pulling my hair from both the front and the back.

Can you detail the extent of this physical violence?

The assault was brutal, swift and systematic. The officers concentrated their blows on my face. They rained heavy punches onto my jaw and my temple. They kicked me repeatedly with their combat boots. The intensity of the physical trauma was overwhelming. Due to the excessive beating, I experienced a temporary loss of consciousness. My body went entirely numb, and the pain briefly stopped registering in my brain. Both of my eyes sustained contusions and structural trauma, which remain visible in subsequent photographs. At around 5:45 pm, they dragged me by the hair and shoved me forcefully into the back of a police vehicle.

What was your experience once you arrived at the Kirtipur Police Circle?

The physical and psychological abuse did not end when the vehicle arrived at the Police Circle. Inside the building, the officers continued to beat me, delivering open-handed slaps and heavy punches to my injured face. They mocked my academic background. They laughed at my injuries and stated tauntingly that they would teach me the true meaning of the law inside the station. They told me they would show me how the Constitution operates in the real world. I attempted to use my mobile phone to contact my family and legal representatives. A police officer stepped forward immediately and threatened me. He stated explicitly that the more phone calls I attempted to make, the more criminal charges they would fabricate against me.

How did you handle the demand to confiscate your phone?

Following the verbal threat, the officer ordered his subordinates to confiscate my mobile phone. I refused to hand over my property. I stated that I would gladly surrender the device, but only after they followed proper legal procedures—a search and seizure memo documenting the confiscation. This insistence made him furious. He lunged forward aggressively as if to strike me down. My friend Monika bravely stepped between us to shield me. She pulled out her own phone to record his violent behaviour. The officers swarmed her, snatching her device and confiscating it without any paperwork. Then, the officer in charge shouted orders to his men to drag us away into the cells.

So you entered the detention cells without a warrant?

I refused to move. I told them that I would not step inside their detention cells unless they presented an arrest warrant. Detaining a citizen without a warrant is a blatant violation of constitutional guarantees. The officer commanded his subordinates to beat us further. I looked him in the eye and told him to issue the arrest warrant first. By this time, I felt as though I was going to collapse. Sarishma informed me that blood was oozing profusely from my face.

Did you receive any medical attention?

Seeing that my face was covered in blood, the police might have realised the risk of custody complications. They held me for another thirty minutes to continue their verbal intimidation, mocking my legal knowledge. They finally transferred me to Kirtipur Hospital for a medical evaluation. The hostility followed me into the medical facility. I was experiencing dizziness and tried to sit on a small stool in the examination area. The medical officer on duty ordered me to stand up immediately. He stated flatly that individuals brought in under police cases have absolutely no right to sit down.

In what way did the hospital administration handle your request for essential medical diagnostics?

I requested the medical officer to document my physical state accurately in my medical history file. He flatly refused to record my statement, claiming it was impossible to write details of the police assault. I was experiencing an agonising headache and feared a brain injury. I begged him for a skull X-ray, stating that I would pay the fees myself. After the hospital staff refused to perform the diagnostic procedure without permission from the detaining guards, I turned to the police officers and pleaded for my life. They granted permission, and I paid for the X-ray.

The X-ray did not show bone fractures, but the pain remained unbearable. The medical staff informed me that my head trauma required an immediate CT scan. Kirtipur Hospital lacked the necessary machinery, and I had to be referred to a specialised hospital. When I asked the guarding personnel what steps we should take, they remained silent. Moments later, their stance shifted entirely. They told me that I was completely free to go wherever and that I was officially released from their custody. They told me to find another hospital on my own. I refused to accept this abandonment.

Since they had arrested me violently and brought me to the hospital in a bloodied state, I would not step outside into the night without a security escort. I managed to use a phone to contact my friends. Advocate Ojaswee Bhattarai and several other supporters arrived at the hospital shortly afterwards. She confronted the police, stating that they could not abandon a severely injured detainee. The police finally relented and allowed an ambulance to transfer me to the Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital (TUTH).

What challenges did you face upon your admission to TUTH?

My friends Sabina Dhakal, Prabhat Labh, and Advocate Akash Mahato accompanied me inside the ambulance. A police officer followed us to the hospital gates but disappeared upon arrival. I was admitted to the emergency ward for three hours before being moved to a cabin at around 11 PM. The doctors confirmed extensive contusions, a heavily swollen jaw, and loose teeth caused by boot strikes. The state did not provide any financial or logistical support. The entire cost of my treatment, amounting to Rs45,000, was covered entirely by me and my friends. I later discovered that while my peers had been released through legal procedures, the state was maintaining a bizarre, unconfirmed hold over me.

Could you explain this ‘hold’?

In the afternoon of the following day, police personnel returned to my cabin. The individual who walked in was the same senior officer who had ordered my confinement at Kirtipur Hospital. He identified himself as an Assistant Sub-Inspector. I confronted him regarding the brutality of his men. He ignored my grievances completely. I then demanded clarification regarding my legal status. I asked him plainly whether I was a prisoner and whether I was under active police control. He looked at me and stated explicitly that I was indeed their prisoner and that I remained under their control. There are multiple witnesses who can confirm this statement.

Did you demand legal paperwork for the hospital detention?

I immediately demanded the corresponding legal paperwork. If I were a prisoner, I would be handed the official arrest and detention documentation. He stated flatly that they were not permitted to give me any paperwork. He told me that I would have to present myself at the police station to sign release documents. I protested against this extrajudicial requirement. I demanded that they either present me before a court of law or hand me over to the National Human Rights Commission.

Did the police officer leave you alone after that?

No, the psychological intimidation intensified that evening. At around 6:20 PM, two plainclothes police officers arrived at the hospital ward. They stationed themselves outside my cabin door and conducted strict surveillance throughout the night. At around 6 AM on Monday, they entered the cabin while I was sleeping and forcibly woke me up to begin a hostile interrogation. My caretakers tried to object, but the officers pushed past them. They demanded to know what specific medications I was taking, who had visited me, and the details of my health. They then stated that a police van was on its way to extract me.

Did the police interfere with your right to legal counsel?

I immediately called my defence lawyer to the hospital cabin. When he arrived, the plainclothes officers treated him with verbal hostility. They refused to allow us to hold a private, confidential legal consultation. They claimed they had strict ‘orders from above’ to remain inside and monitor every single word spoken between me and my lawyer. This was a blatant violation of constitutional guarantees. The confrontation lasted until the hospital doctors and administration intervened. The medical staff told the police that they were jeopardising my health and ordered them to leave the ward immediately. The police finally retreated but continued their surveillance.

Will you be facing legal charges from the police?

I have received reliable information that the police are planning to file charges of ‘indecent behaviour’ against me. This specific charge is an arbitrary tool used by the state to muzzle civilian dissent and suppress freedom of expression. Under this charge, the police do not need to present the accused before a court to secure a detention extension. They simply require permission from the Chief District Officer, who routinely approves such extensions without judicial oversight. A citizen can be held in police custody for weeks before their case ever reaches a court. The pre-trial detention itself serves as an immediate, unappealable punishment.

How does your experience reflect the wider systemic issues within the security apparatus?

The entire security apparatus is in desperate need of comprehensive reform. There is no viable legal recourse for citizens when police press arbitrary charges. This systemic unchecked power extends from political detentions to daily traffic enforcement. When the traffic or municipal police issue arbitrary fines or seize property, citizens have no independent tribunal for appeal. This complete lack of legal recourse can have fatal consequences. We saw this clearly in the tragic self-immolation of Ganesh Nepali. The city police wheel-locked his motorcycle and imposed an arbitrary fine. He had zero legal channels to appeal their decision. My brutal beating is a product of this exact same unchecked state violence.

How do you view the wave of online hostility and Islamophobia that followed your arrest?

The reaction across major social media platforms has been deeply alarming. The comment sections under the news portals are flooded with vile, Islamophobic slurs. This is not an organic reaction from the general public. This is a highly coordinated digital campaign executed by a state-sponsored cyber army. Conversely, my personal profiles are filled with genuine messages of solidarity from real citizens.

Do you think that there was government complicity in your mistreatment?

The complicity and awareness of this violence extend directly to the highest political offices in the country. Following my illegal arrest and hospitalisation, my friend Bhawana Raut published a detailed post on social media condemning the police brutality. The Minister for Home Affairs, Sudan Gurung, reacted to that specific post using a ‘Haha’ emoji. This reaction is a piece of evidence. It suggests that the head of security is fully aware of the extrajudicial violence being carried out by his subordinates. Instead of initiating an investigation, he chose to publicly mock the physical trauma.

How has this ordeal affected your family and community?

I am the only member of my entire family who has ever had the privilege of receiving a higher education. They placed all their hopes and pride in my academic journey. The news of my assault and detention left them devastated. To make matters worse, several of my friends in Morang organised a peaceful protest to demand my release. The police cracked down on them, detaining them overnight. They were only released after being forced to sign a written commitment promising never to hold protests again. The regime is actively suppressing dissent nationwide.

What are your demands from the state?

I refuse to be silenced by their boots, their threats, or their cyber armies. Today it is me, but tomorrow this authoritarian regime will target another citizen. They are systematic in their censorship. I am officially demanding a full, independent investigation into the actions of the Kirtipur police. The officers involved in assaulting me must face criminal prosecution. I demand a formal guarantee of my personal security, individual freedom, and protection from extrajudicial detention.

Do you believe that the Supreme Court writ petition you filed is the primary catalyst for this violence?

Yes, I am absolutely certain of it. My legal activism on behalf of the evicted squatter settlers is the reason why I was singled out for this brutal treatment. The Supreme Court writ petition, registered under code 082-WO-1237, directly challenges the state’s illegal management of evicted squatter settlers. By filing this lawsuit, we forced the government to answer for its systemic failures. Authoritarian regimes are inherently terrified of the law. They are terrified of citizens who understand their constitutional rights and refuse to be intimidated. They realised they could not defeat our legal arguments in a courtroom, so they resorted to physical violence to break our bodies and silence our voices. But they have failed completely.

articles.title: Judiciary left reeling from Gen Z protest impact as case clearance almost halved
articles.summary:
The Gen Z protests that swept across the country on September 8 and 9 last year have severely hit the country’s judicial system. With courts operating under significant limitations, the national case clearance rate plummeted to just 55 percent in the fiscal year 2025-2026.

According to the Supreme Court, out of the 357,023 pending cases lodged with various tiers across the country, only 196,474 were settled, leaving a backlog of 160,549 cases. This marks a sharp decline from the previous year’s overall clearance rate of 65.69 percent.

The Supreme Court recorded the lowest performance, settling only 29.46 percent of its cases in 2025-26, compared to 42 percent in 2024-25. High courts wrapped up 70.36 percent of their caseload against 74.61 percent previously, while district courts resolved 55.61 percent, down from 66.25 percent. Other tribunals managed to settle 41.67 percent, a major drop from last year's 56.34 percent.

Various reports show that the nationwide Gen Z protests caused an estimated total economic loss of Rs84.5 billion, with the judiciary bearing a heavy blow. Protesters destroyed or burnt approximately 936,000 legal case files and documents, crippling ongoing litigations.

The structural damage to the judiciary alone was estimated at Rs2.8 billion. A total of 23 court premises were struck, including the Supreme Court, the Special Court, seven high courts, and 14 district courts. Among them, 10 buildings were completely destroyed, nine suffered partial damage, and four sustained minor issues.

The Supreme Court sustained the heaviest blow, with its main historical building heavily ruined, resulting in losses worth Rs1.23 billion. Across the nation, infrastructure damage stood at Rs1.65 billion, vehicle losses amounted to Rs615.1 million, and office equipment damage totalled Rs538.5 million.

Supreme Court spokesperson Arjun Koirala stated that judicial activities remained virtually suspended for nearly four months after the movement. "The destruction of vital files and court property brought hearings to a standstill," said Koirala. "Severe damage to our central servers disrupted systems nationwide, preventing the judiciary from achieving its yearly targets."

Even courts that escaped direct vandalism suffered from the technological breakdown. Lal Bahadur Kunwar, acting Chief Judge of the Patan High Court, explained that the technical fallout halted their work for two months. "Although our buildings were not physically attacked, the loss of central databases and files from other courts left us unable to conduct full hearings," said Kunwar.

Special Court Chairman Sudarshan Dev Bhatta also linked the performance drop to the structural challenges. "The combination of the September riots, infrastructure loss, and scheduled judge transfers hindered our efficiency," said Bhatta. "It took substantial time to restore essential IT equipment and servers destroyed in the fire."

Bhatta added that thanks to collaborative recovery efforts, the Special Court was restored within four months, allowing them to initiate a targeted campaign to clear backlogs. The Special Court eventually settled 155 out of 261 cases, achieving a 59.38 percent resolution rate, with 106 cases remaining.

Top-performing judges by case disposal

Despite the operational challenges, several judges managed to achieve high performance numbers. In the High Court category, Judge Tek Narayan Kunwar recorded the highest number of settlements. Known for introducing digital initiatives and modern e-courts during his previous tenure at the Special Court in Kathmandu, Kunwar maintained his quick pace after his transfer to the Janakpur High Court.

Other top-performing High Court judges included Tikaram Acharya, Jagat Bahadur Thapa, Somkant Mainali, Narishwar Bhandari, Jagadish Ghimire, Gokarna Dangi, Krishna Prasad Subedi, Rajuram Silwal, and Kailash Prasad Subedi.

At the district level, Judge Rajendra Singh Bhandari of the Kanchanpur District Court led the list for the highest number of verdicts. He was followed by Madhav Prasad Ghimire, Hari Prasad Sharma Upadhyay, Kapil Mani Gautam, Bishnu Prasad Gautam, Roshan Gajurel, Manoj KC, Durga Bahadur Bhusal, Manoj Kumar Srivastava, and Bhuwan Singh Thapa.

articles.title: Who will save libraries?
articles.summary:
Once, libraries were hubs of learning and engaging places for individuals to exchange ideas. Despite the politically challenging times of the Panchayat era, libraries flourished, and so did the habit of visiting them. But decades of official neglect and declining public investment have pushed many libraries to the brink of extinction. The closure of the Kathmandu Valley Public Library at Bhrikutimandap is a telling example. The Social Welfare Council, which manages the library, shut it down in April, citing unpaid rent of around Rs30 million. While the unpaid dues have been presented as the immediate cause, the closure ultimately reflects the government’s failure to recognise and protect libraries as essential public institutions. Instead of finding ways to further promote a library that housed around 60,000 books, journals, reports and booklets, served some 3,000 members and attracted around 200 daily visitors, authorities chose to shut it down.

Policymakers often speak of taking education to new heights, but the ambition rings hollow when a public library serving those who cannot afford expensive books, academic journals or reliable internet services is forced to shut down. Despite the rise of mobile phones, the internet and digital resources, the importance of libraries has not reduced. We just need to look at well-managed libraries such as the Nepal National Library, the Kaiser Library, and the Tribhuvan University Central Library to understand the importance of libraries even today. A large number of people throng these reading spaces as not everyone has the privilege of having a library-like environment at home or in the rooms they rent. Often, it is easy to access reference materials and books from libraries and read in their quiet corners.

Nepal should therefore rethink the role of public libraries. In the past, during the Rana regime, people fought for intellectual freedom, demanding knowledge that would be accessible to all. That history deserves to be remembered. Today, people have more access to knowledge, but many libraries continue to operate as they did decades ago, failing to adapt to the changes in how people learn. So, they should be equipped with both traditional collections and digital catalogues, e-books, academic databases, multimedia resources and high-speed internet services.

The responsibility of managing libraries should extend beyond the federal government. Many community libraries in the country were established by passionate founders and activists or through community initiatives. Now, they reportedly struggle to survive due to a lack of resources. Municipalities and communities should therefore recognise libraries as essential public spaces and invest in them. The private sector can also collaborate by investing in technology and library resources. The country desperately needs a vision for public libraries that meets the demands of modern learning practices while preserving their fundamental value.

Several countries around the world continue to expand public libraries as community learning centres, digital resource hubs and cultural spaces. They subsidise libraries to make them accessible to all, acknowledging that their purpose is to generate knowledge. Their practice is worth emulating. However, Nepal, with the recent closure of a library due to unpaid rent, is moving in the opposite direction. The current government boasts a Cabinet and Parliament filled with ‘intellectual’ and ‘educated’ individuals. Such a government has a greater responsibility to protect institutions of learning. If they cannot save libraries, it is difficult to imagine who will.

articles.title: सुन्दर सूर्यविनायकलाई फोहोरमैलाको चुनौती
articles.summary:
भक्तपुरको प्राकृतिक रूपमा अत्यन्तै सुन्दर र पर्यटकीय सम्भावना बोकेको सूर्यविनायक नगरपालिका क्षेत्र यतिबेला फोहोरमैला व्यवस्थापनको संकटबाट गुज्रिरहेको छ।
